title: Trigger Finger and Common Finger Tendon Injuries

rows: Thickened flexor tendon or A1 pulley; the tendon catches as the finger bends and straightens
Extensor tendon torn or avulsed at the end joint; fingertip droops
Central slip of extensor torn over the middle joint; PIP flexes, DIP hyperextends
Blow to the PIP or laceration
Flexor digitorum profundus avulsed from the fingertip; cannot bend the end joint
Grabbing a jersey in sport (often ring finger)

sections.title: B to C. Presentation and key questions

items: Trigger finger: clicking, catching or locking, often worse in the morning, tender nodule at the base of the finger in the palm.
Mallet: drooping fingertip, cannot actively straighten it.
Ask about the mechanism, onset, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and any surgery.

rows: Press at the palmar base of the finger while the patient flexes and extends
Tender nodule or palpable catching: trigger finger
Hold the middle phalanx; patient straightens the fingertip
Bend the PIP 90 degrees over a table edge; patient extends the PIP against resistance
Weak PIP extension with DIP rigidity: central slip injury
Hold the PIP straight; patient bends the fingertip
Hold the other fingers straight; patient bends the tested finger
Unable to flex the PIP: FDS injury

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Unable to flex fingertip after a pull injury
Penetrating injury with loss of flexion or numbness
Red, swollen finger, pain on passive extension, held flexed

steps: **Acute injury with loss of active movement?** Identify the tendon; jersey finger and lacerations go to the hand surgeon urgently.
**Mallet finger:** continuous extension splint for the DIP.
**Trigger finger:** splint and activity change; refer for injection if persistent.

rows: Splint holding the MCP joint in slight extension (often night use), reduce forceful gripping, tendon gliding. Corticosteroid injection by a doctor is effective for many [Ref – to verify]; release surgery if persistent

DIP extension splint worn continuously for about 6 to 8 weeks, then gradual weaning at night [Ref – to verify]. The fingertip must never bend during this time, even during skin care: support it flat on a table while changing the splint
PIP extension splint with DIP free and active DIP flexion exercises

Follow the surgical protocol strictly (early active or controlled motion program in a dorsal blocking splint). Never perform resisted flexion or passive extension early; rupture risk is highest in the first weeks

blocks.text: Active range (total active motion), triggering frequency, extension lag, grip, function.

items: **Why must a mallet finger splint never be removed with the tip unsupported?** Any bending can disrupt healing and restart the timeline.
**Which test isolates FDP?** Holding the PIP straight while the patient flexes the DIP.
**Why is jersey finger urgent?** The tendon can retract; delay makes repair difficult.
**Which condition gives a flexed PIP and hyperextended DIP?** Boutonniere deformity.
**After flexor tendon repair, what is forbidden early?** Resisted flexion and passive finger extension with the wrist extended.
